from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Three-Dimensional Linear Transformations", [
            "Linear transformations generalize 2D to 3D.",
            "Any vector is built from basis vectors i, j, k.",
            "We define 3D space with a coordinate grid.",
            "Visualize the unit cube.",
            "Show grid components."
        ])
        
        # Define mobjects
        vector_v = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=UP*1.5+RIGHT*1, color=YELLOW)
        matrix_a = MathTex(r"A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}", color=BLUE)
        result_av = MathTex(r"Av = v'", color=ORANGE)
        
        # --- Animations ---
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.place_at_grid(vector_v, 'C3')
        self.play(Create(vector_v))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.place_at_grid(matrix_a, 'B5')
        self.play(FadeIn(matrix_a))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(ORANGE))
        self.place_at_grid(result_av, 'E3')
        self.play(Write(result_av))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        # Logic for cube as placeholder for [Asset: unit_cube_i_j_k]
        cube = Cube(side_length=1.5, fill_opacity=0.3, color=GREEN)
        self.place_at_grid(cube, 'E5')
        self.play(Create(cube))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(RED))
        self.play(Indicate(vector_v), Indicate(result_av))

sections.title: Prerequisites & Intuition (1:00)
sections.content: Brief review of 2D linear transformations (matrix-vector multiplication) and the basis vectors i, j, k. Introduce 3D space as a grid of vectors where any point is defined by its coordinates (x, y, z).
sections.example: Visualizing a 3D unit cube composed of vectors i(1,0,0), j(0,1,0), and k(0,0,1) anchored at the origin.

sections.title: The Matrix Representation (1:00)
sections.content: Explain that a 3D transformation is defined by where the basis vectors land. A 3x3 matrix tracks the new positions of i, j, and k. The columns of the matrix represent these transformed basis vectors.
sections.example: A 'Robot Arm' character: The matrix columns describe how the arm's base (i), mid-section (j), and gripper (k) are oriented in 3D space after rotation.

sections.title: Visualizing Transformations (1:30)
sections.content: Demonstrate the three primary types of transformations: Scaling (stretching along axes), Rotation (rotating around an axis), and Shearing. Show how these change the 'grid' of the entire 3D space.
sections.example: A 'Digital Character' model: Scaling it to make it taller, rotating it to face the camera, and shearing to create a 'speed effect' or slant.

sections.title: Determinants & Invertibility (1:00)
sections.content: Define the determinant as the 'volume scaling factor.' Explain that if the determinant is zero, the 3D space collapses into a 2D plane or 1D line, losing information.
sections.example: A 'Space-Folding Device': If the determinant is zero, a 3D object inside the device is flattened into a 'paper-thin' 2D shape, illustrating loss of dimensionality.

sections.title: Summary & Application (0:30)
sections.content: Recap: Linear transformations are matrix-vector products. They are the engine behind 3D computer graphics, game engine physics, and robotics movement.
sections.example: The final assembly of a 3D character game engine: Matrix multiplication transforms the character from local model space into the global game world.
